I absolutely hate it when people try to translate Mandarin according to the Pinyin. Without the tonal marks you have no idea what that's saying. Even with the tonal marks, good luck. Pinyin is not Chinese.

份 (fèn) is the classifier for gifts, newspapers, reports, contracts and such documents of which multiple copies can be produced. Off the top of my head I don't know what would be the classifier for smells, but I'm pretty sure it's not that.

一 (yī, one) 份 would be roughly "a copy of chou" ... whatever chou is.

I looked up the sound chou in my dictionary and there's no word there that would use the 份 classifier.

There is an yì​fèn though, 义愤, which means roughly a sense of indignation. There is 仇 (chóu), which is anger, and 抽 (chōu) which means roughly to draw something out of a whole. I'm only familiar with that character in one context though (the verb to smoke, as in a cigarette) so I can't really explain further. However, that might be more in line with what the author intended for his pen name. In English, the name would be Chou Yifen which would translate literally as 'to draw out righteous anger.' The dash suggests to me yì​fèn, rather than yī fèn. They do that sometimes so whiteys not in the know don't pronounce something stupid like 'yiffen.'

It could be a whole different fen sound, too, a character I don't know.

It could be just a name with no inherent meaning. Again, Pinyin is not Chinese.

I do actually kinda know Chinese though, and I'm sure it's not 'a piece of stink.' Wrong classifier.
